title: Aquinas: it all seems like straw
hook: after an experience at Mass he stopped writing, saying all his work seemed like straw

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dumb ox, the quiet student in the back. Your line was the ox will bellow. Who did you ask a real question, and did you wait for the answer? Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Straw. That's the word he used. The quiet student has grown into a great teacher. For years he has been writing a vast work explaining the Christian faith, question by question, answer by answer, dictating to helpers. Then one morning in Naples he says Mass, and something happens. The sources never say what. Afterward he puts down his pen. He won't write. He won't dictate. His friend and companion, Reginald, begs him to go on. And Thomas gives him a strange answer. Today: Aquinas, and the straw.

The account comes from testimony gathered after his death, when the church was looking into his life. Reginald presses him: why stop now? And Thomas says, in effect: I can't. Everything I have written seems like straw to me, compared with what I have seen. That's the whole story. He never says what he saw. He doesn't explain it, write it up or teach it. The great work, the one people still call the Summa, is left unfinished. He dies not long after, on a journey. What do you do with that? First, notice what he did not say. He did not say his work was false. He did not say burn it. Straw is not poison. Straw is what grain grows on. It holds the wheat up, and then the harvest is gathered and the straw is left in the field. The church kept reading him, and still does. Second, notice where it happened: at Mass, in prayer, not at a desk. Thomas had spent his life using reason to speak about God, and he believed reason was a gift. But Paul had already said that our knowing has a limit: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Some readers hear in the straw a man who glimpsed the face. Some readers also wonder whether he was ill or worn out, and say both could be true at once. The sources don't settle it. What they leave us is a teacher who stopped talking, and left a silence where the rest of his book should be.
screen: `STRAW, COMPARED WITH WHAT I HAVE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop, and let silence speak. Settle, and breathe. Put down whatever you're holding, the phone, the pen, the plan for the next hour. For this minute, add no words of your own. No explaining. No commentary in your head, or as little as you can manage. When a thought comes, let it go by like a cart on a far road. If you pray, you can sit with a line from the prophet Habakkuk: let all the earth keep silence before him. If you don't, just let the quiet be full. The bell holds the time.
Aquinas. Thomas Aquinas, the teacher who explained the faith question by question, and then stopped writing, saying it all seemed like straw beside what he had seen.
Your line: all is straw. Today, when you catch yourself explaining something a third time, stop, and let a little silence do the work. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Catholic students and teachers still study the Summa Theologiae, and the story of the straw is told in retreats and sermons about the limits of words before God.

fork.setup: you're Reginald. your friend Thomas has stopped writing his great work and won't say why. what do you do?
options: finish it for him without asking.
press him to go on, and ask why he stopped.
leave quietly and tell no one.
fork.reveal: Reginald begs him to go on. Thomas answers that all he has written seems like straw compared with what he has seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a great thinker decided his work was worthless.
what it means: after something at Mass, Thomas stopped writing. his words seemed like straw beside what he had seen, not false, just small.
what a scholar hears: Bartholomew of Capua's testimony in the canonization inquiry, reporting what Reginald told him; the Summa's third part breaks off unfinished.

sources.ref: Testimony of Bartholomew of Capua, Naples canonization inquiry for Thomas Aquinas

notes: The straw story is paraphrased from Bartholomew of Capua's testimony (relayed from Reginald of Piperno). The Mass is placed in Naples without a date (the feast of St. Nicholas is left out). Confirm.
'Dictating to helpers sometimes faster than they can write' draws on the early lives' accounts of dictating to several secretaries; confirm or cut.
'He dies not long after, on a journey' (en route to the Council of Lyon, at Fossanova); no date given. Confirm.
The straw-and-wheat image is the script's own reading, offered as a picture, not attributed to Thomas.
'Some readers also wonder whether he was ill' refers to modern suggestions of a stroke or breakdown; framed as some readers, not ranked.
Habakkuk 2:20 paraphrased in the practice (without quotation marks).
Editor: cut 'faster than they can write' and 'nobody in the room can say what' (not in the cited testimony).
